cover_design.label: MALAY
cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Malay for complete beginners — from teh tarik at the mamak stall to a formal letter that gets results in Kuala Lumpur.
cover_design.catatan: Every line of dialogue comes with a word-for-word translation and an English-friendly pronunciation guide.

product.title: Malay 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Malay: real dialogues, word-for-word translations, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises and an answer key. Malay is one of the friendliest languages an English speaker can pick up — no verb conjugation, no gender, no tones, a Latin alphabet spelled the way it sounds, and hundreds of words borrowed from English (bas, teksi, universiti, stesen). This course focuses on what actually trips learners up: the Johor-Riau pronunciation that turns 'apa' into 'apə', the particles -lah and ke that decide whether you sound polite or blunt, the colloquial Malay (tak, nak, kat, je, dah) people really speak, words that mean something quite different in Indonesian, and a full unit on Jawi script so the signboards in Kelantan stop being pictures. The dialogues follow an Indonesian student who has just landed in Kuala Lumpur, and they deliberately cover everyday things: teh tarik at the mamak stall, toilets at the LRT station, forms at the bank, wedding invitations.

blocks.text: Malay is the national language of Malaysia and Brunei, one of the four official languages of Singapore, and — in its Indonesian form — the everyday language of well over two hundred million people. **Bahasa Melayu** (Malaysian Malay) and **Bahasa Indonesia** are two standard varieties of one language, split not by ancestry but by two different colonial histories and two different modern states. This course teaches the Malaysian standard.

For an English speaker, the good news starts on page one. There is no verb conjugation, no grammatical gender, no case endings, and plurals don't change the shape of a word. The word order is the one you already use: subject, verb, object, with time and place tacked on at the end. Words are built with a handful of regular prefixes and suffixes — *me-*, *ber-*, *di-*, *-kan*, *-an* — that work the same way every time.
What trips learners up isn't grammar. It's four other things, and this course is built around all four.

items: **False friends with Indonesian.** Many words are spelled exactly the same in Malaysia and Indonesia but mean something different — sometimes very different, sometimes embarrassingly so. *Percuma* means "free of charge" in Malaysia but "pointless" in Indonesia. *Kereta* means "car", not "train". *Budak* means "child", not "slave". Indonesian films, music and tourists are everywhere in Malaysia, so you will meet both meanings; this course gives the topic a whole unit and a reference list at the back.

**Pronunciation.** Malay spelling is regular, but Malaysians don't say the final *a* the way it's written. Words ending in *a* — *apa, saya, kita, nama, bila, mana* — end in a short "uh": **ah-puh, sah-yuh, kee-tuh**. A final *r* almost disappears: *besar* comes out as **buh-sah**. Learn these two habits and suddenly you can hear words you already know.

**Loanwords from English.** Malay has borrowed hundreds of words from English and Arabic and spelled them the Malay way: *stesen* (station), *hospital*, *farmasi* (pharmacy), *basikal* (bicycle), *teksi* (taxi), *universiti*. For an English speaker this is a gift — once you know the spelling patterns, you can read hundreds of words you were never taught.

**Colloquial Malay.** What's printed in the newspaper isn't what you hear at the *mamak* stall. *Tidak* becomes *tak*, *hendak* becomes *nak*, *di* becomes *kat*, *sahaja* becomes *je*, *sudah* becomes *dah*, and almost every sentence ends in *-lah* or *kan?*. Without this layer you can read a Malaysian newspaper but can't follow the conversation at the next table.

blocks.text: Because the grammar is so light, this course moves faster than most. Unit 1 already has a full ten-line dialogue. The word-for-word translation is printed under every line so you can see exactly **how a Malay sentence is put together** — which words it leaves out, which particles it adds, and where it simply takes a different road from English.

The dialogues follow **Sarah**, an Indonesian student who has just landed in Kuala Lumpur to study, together with **Haziq** and **Aina**, two Malaysians who take her under their wing, and now and then **Pak Cik Rosli**, who runs the shop below the student residence. What they talk about is deliberately ordinary: finding the toilet, ordering *teh tarik*, taking the LRT, filling in a bank form, going to a wedding feast. The language people really use is the language of ordinary things.

Twenty units, one dialogue each, about twenty to thirty minutes a sitting. Many learners finish in five to six weeks. By the last page you won't be Malaysian — but you'll be able to get through a day in Malaysia in Malay, and you'll understand much of what you hear around you. *Selamat maju jaya* — all the best on your way.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place. If you only have time for three units, take units 1, 3 and 12.

blocks.text: This course is written to be used on your own, without a teacher. Every unit follows the same order, and that order is no accident — it copies the way people actually pick up a language: **listen to the whole thing first, then take it apart, then use it.**

items: **Dialogue.** Read it once without looking at the translation and see how much you can guess from context and from words borrowed from English. Then read the English translation.

**Word-for-word translation** (the small line marked *literally:*). It shows how the Malay sentence is built: the missing "is" and "a", the particles with no English equivalent, the words in a different order.
**Notes.** The heart of the course. This is where false friends are exposed, pronunciation is explained, and habits from English that you need to drop are named plainly.
**Grammar boxes.** Short, set out in tables, and focused on what Malay does differently from English.
**Vocabulary.** Three columns: the Malay word, how to say it, and the English meaning. ⚠️ marks a word that means something different in Indonesian.
**Exercises and answer key.** Do them on paper, not in your head. The answers are in the grey box right below — cover it with your hand first.

blocks.title: Three signs used throughout the course
items: **Bold** — the word or part under discussion at that point.
*Italics* — a Malay word or sentence quoted in the middle of an English sentence.
**uh** — in the "Say it" column, the short neutral vowel of *about* (written *ə* by linguists). It's the sound you'll see most often there, and the next chapter explains why.

blocks.text: One piece of advice language courses rarely give: **don't translate in your head.** Malay sentences are short and leave out words English insists on ("is", "a", "the", "will"). If you keep rebuilding every sentence in English you'll stay stuck at "I understand but can't say it". Treat Malay as its own system with its own logic.

If you want to train your ear while you read, this course can also be opened in the Linguo app: tap any Malay word to hear it. For Malay this is more useful than usual — reading is easy; your real challenge is hearing.

Malay uses the Latin alphabet and is spelled almost exactly as it sounds. The vowels are pure: **a** as in *father* ("ah"), **i** as in *machine* ("ee"), **u** as in *food* ("oo"), **o** as in *more* ("oh"), and **e** is usually a short "uh" (*about*), sometimes "eh" (*bed*). **c** is always "ch", **g** is always hard, **ng** is the sound in *singer* (even at the start of a word), **ny** as in *canyon*, **sy** = "sh", **kh** a throaty "h", and a final **k** is just a catch in the throat (*budak* ≈ boo-dah'). There is no stress that changes meaning: give every syllable roughly equal weight. On top of that, four habits matter in almost every sentence — read this chapter carefully and come back to it as often as you need.
1. A final *a* becomes "uh"

This is the biggest, most frequent difference between how Malay is written and how it's said. Malaysians (and Singaporeans, and most Bruneians) pronounce a word-final *a* as a short **uh**, like the *a* in *sofa*:

Note that **only the very last *a*** changes. An *a* in the middle of a word stays a full "ah": *bahasa* is **bah-hah-suh**, not "buh-huh-suh". And a word that doesn't end in *a* — *masyarakat* (society) — doesn't change at all.

This is called the **Johor-Riau pronunciation**, after the Malay dialect of Johor and the Riau Islands that became the standard. Between 1988 and 2000, Malaysia officially switched to a **"spelling pronunciation"** — every letter read as written, *apa* as "ah-pah", much as Indonesians say it — and all TV broadcasts used it. People never took to it; in 2000 the policy was dropped and Johor-Riau was restored. If you watch Malaysian TV recordings from the 90s and think "this sounds strangely Indonesian", that's why.

blocks.title: The good news
items: You **don't have to** copy it. Malaysians fully understand "ah-pah" with a full *a* — they hear Indonesian every day in songs, films and social media.
What you **do** need is to **recognize it when you hear it**. Learners almost always struggle with their ears, not their mouths.
If you decide to copy it, go all the way — not halfway. Half Johor-Riau sounds much odder than a consistent letter-by-letter reading.

blocks.text: 2. A final *r* almost disappears
The partner of habit 1. An *r* closing the last syllable isn't rolled; it melts into the vowel before it, much as in British English (*car*, *father*).

Put the two rules together and you'll see why *besar sangat* (very big) comes out as **buh-sah sah-ngaht** and *kereta besar* (a big car) as **kuh-reh-tuh buh-sah**. Two rules, and Malay already sounds different from what the spelling made you expect.
3. The letter *e* has two sounds

Malay spelling uses one letter *e* for two sounds: the short **uh** (b**e**sar, k**e**cil, s**e**but — the "pepet" e) and **eh** as in *bed* (m**e**ja, s**e**lera, b**e**ca — the "taling" e). The spelling doesn't tell you which, but in this course the "Say it" column always does: *besar* = **buh-sah**, *meja* = **meh-juh**. The short "uh" is far more common, so it's the safe guess.
4. English loanwords are said the Malay way, not the English way
Malay has borrowed thousands of words from English and respelled them until they sound fully Malay. Don't say them as in English — that actually sounds wrong. Say them as written, with Malay vowels.

Notice the spelling patterns: English *-ty* becomes **-ti** (*universiti, kualiti, komuniti, fakulti*), *-tion* becomes **-sen** or **-si** (*stesen*, *stesyen*; *informasi*), *-sion* becomes **-syen** (*televisyen*). Once you spot the patterns, hundreds of words read themselves.
What you DON'T need to learn

To show how much you're spared, here is what usually eats up the first weeks of other languages and doesn't appear here at all: word stress that changes meaning (none), tones (none), long and short vowels that change meaning (none), accented letters (none), verb endings (none), grammatical gender (none) — and no new script, unless you choose to open unit 19, where Jawi script awaits.

This page is short on purpose, and that's the point: Malay grammar is light. Gathered here are only the points that work **differently** from English — the pronouns, the polite titles, the negatives, the time words and the particles you'll use every day.

blocks.text: Titles — what people actually say
In polite Malaysian conversation, pronouns are often replaced with **titles**, the way English uses "sir" or "ma'am" — only much more often, and right in the middle of the sentence.

Particles — the genuinely new part
Five words that work differently than you'd expect

items: **boleh** = can, be able to (not just "may"). *Saya boleh cakap Melayu* = I can speak Malay. ⚠️ The word *bisa* in Malay means **venom** — in Indonesian it means "can".
**kena** = have to, must; also "get hit by". *Saya kena pergi* = I have to go. *Dia kena denda* = he got fined.
**nak** (from *hendak*) = want, be going to. *Nak makan apa?* = what do you want to eat?
**sila** = please (inviting someone). *Tolong* = please (asking for help). Don't mix them up: *Sila duduk* is right; *Tolong duduk* sounds like an order.
**buat** = for (as well as "to make, to do"). *Ini buat awak* = this is for you.

blocks.text: *Ialah* and *adalah* — Malay's "is"
Malay normally needs no word for "is". In formal standard Malay, though, two linking words are used, and Malaysian schools test the difference:

head: Word
Followed by
Example
rows: Cuaca hari ini **adalah** panas. · Buku itu **adalah** untuk awak.

blocks.text: In conversation both are usually dropped — *Ibu kota Malaysia Kuala Lumpur* ("The capital of Malaysia [is] Kuala Lumpur"). The rule only matters when you write formally.

A reference page for anyone who will also hear Indonesian — on Malaysian TV, in Indonesian songs and films, or on a trip to Bali. Every word below is **spelled the same** in both countries but means something different. 🔴 marks words that aren't just confusing but can embarrass or offend.

blocks.text: A survival rule for words that aren't on this list: **if a word sounds odd where it is, don't guess — ask.** You only need one rescue sentence, and Malaysians will be glad to answer it: *Maaf, dalam bahasa Melayu, perkataan ini maksudnya apa?* (Sorry, in Malay, what does this word mean?)

If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, you're past the hardest stretch. You know which words not to use, your ear accepts *ah-puh* for *apa* and *buh-sah* for *besar* without stumbling, and you can order food, take the LRT, fill in a form and reply to an invitation without sounding like a machine translation.
Three things that will raise your level fastest

items: **Watch the news, not dramas.** TV3's *Buletin Utama* and RTM's *Berita* use clear standard Malay at a moderate pace, on topics you already know about. Dramas are full of colloquial and regional Malay — great later, too heavy for now.

**Read the papers online.** *Berita Harian*, *Utusan Malaysia*, *Harian Metro* or *Astro Awani*. Malaysian newspaper language is compact, and it's where the official and administrative vocabulary you don't have yet is concentrated.

**Find people to talk to, not more books.** Malay grammar is light, so what holds you back isn't knowledge but habit — and habits only change through use. Ten minutes of chatting with a Malaysian teaches more than ten pages of word lists.

blocks.text: If you want an official exam

There's no single international Malay exam as well known as TOEFL or JLPT, so the route depends on your goal. **Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka (DBP)** is Malaysia's official language institute and publishes the standard references — *Kamus Dewan* is the dictionary everyone cites, and its online version is free. For school and work in Malaysia, the **SPM Bahasa Melayu** paper is the best-known benchmark. For university, each institution sets its own language requirements — check directly with the faculty, as they vary and change.
If you want to explore other varieties

Malay isn't one single thing. What you've learned here is **standard Malaysian Malay** — the Malay of schools, newspapers and official business in Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore. Beyond it lies a big world: **Brunei Malay** with its own court vocabulary, **Kelantan-Patani Malay**, which sounds so different that even people from Kuala Lumpur need time, **Sarawak** and **Sabah Malay** with their layer of Borneo words, **Singapore Malay**, mixed on the street with English, Hokkien and Tamil — and, of course, **Indonesian**, the variety spoken by more people than all the others combined.
All of them are open to you now, and all of them are closer than you might think. *Selamat maju jaya, dan jumpa lagi* — all the best, and see you again.
